Libya’s National Oil Corp Enters Insolvency, Disrupting Operations Across Key Oil Fields

TRIPOLI, June 19 – National Oil Corp, Libya’s largest state-run oil producer, has entered insolvency proceedings, disrupting oil production and raising concerns over the country’s vital energy sector, company officials and industry analysts said Wednesday.

The company confirmed in a statement that it had filed for insolvency late Tuesday, after months of mounting debts and cash flow difficulties. “We regret to inform our partners and the Libyan public that National Oil Corp is now under insolvency administration,” a spokesperson said. “We are working closely with administrators to assess the company’s assets and liabilities, and to determine next steps.”

Immediate effects have rippled through Libya’s oil industry, with local union representatives reporting that operations at several key fields—including the Sharara and Sarir fields—have been partially suspended. “Hundreds of workers have been sent home until further notice,” said Khaled Hamed, head of the Petroleum Workers’ Union. “The situation is very uncertain, and we are concerned about the future of our members’ jobs.”

National Oil Corp is a backbone of Libya’s economy, contributing over 70% of government revenue in recent years. The company had been struggling to maintain production amid political instability, delayed payments from overseas buyers, and infrastructure challenges. According to internal figures seen by industry analysts, crude oil output has fallen by nearly 40% since January, with daily production now estimated at about 650,000 barrels.

“This insolvency is a blow not just to the company, but to the whole Libyan economy,” said Amal Farouk, an energy analyst at the Tripoli-based consultancy North Africa Energy Insight. “Without urgent intervention, we could see further declines in production and export capacity.”

The Ministry of Oil and Gas said it was monitoring the situation and considering options for restructuring or partially privatizing some assets. “We are committed to safeguarding the interests of Libya and its people,” the ministry said in a brief statement.

As of Wednesday afternoon, administrators were meeting with creditors and government officials to discuss potential paths forward. Operations at many of National Oil Corp’s facilities remained suspended or significantly reduced.
